summary:
John Bercow (born 1963) is a British former Conservative MP who served as Speaker of the House of Commons from 2009 to 2019. He represented Buckingham from 1997 until leaving Parliament, and was the first Speaker since the Second World War to be elected four times.

After studying government at the University of Essex, Bercow worked in Conservative politics, served as a Lambeth councillor and unsuccessfully stood for Parliament twice before winning Buckingham. He rose through the Conservative front bench, but resigned in 2002 over the party’s opposition to a bill allowing unmarried couples to adopt, and was dismissed from the shadow cabinet in 2004 after clashing with leader Michael Howard. Though initially associated with the party’s right wing, his views later shifted, prompting speculation that he might join Labour.

Elected Speaker after Michael Martin resigned, Bercow left the Conservative Party, as convention requires, and served as an independent. His tenure included efforts to increase MPs’ influence and high-profile involvement in parliamentary debates, including those surrounding Brexit. He also chaired the UK Youth Parliament’s annual sitting. His speakership drew criticism over the refurbishment of his parliamentary residence and claims concerning his expenses; he denied wrongdoing in the expenses controversy and repaid money to cover potential tax liability.

Bercow announced in 2019 that he would step down as Speaker and MP. After Parliament, he held university roles, including chancellor of the universities of Bedfordshire and Essex, and became a part-time politics professor at Royal Holloway. He joined the Labour Party in 2021, but was suspended in 2022 after complaints of bullying were upheld. Bercow has also supported charities and received recognition for his work on LGBT equality.
